information; failure to respond can lead to restrictions being placed on the relevant shares. PSC
particulars are filed with the Registrar, and since 18 November 2025 individual PSCs must verify their
identity.

## Partnership and LLP decision-making

The specification names "partnership decision-making and authority of partners" separately, and the
rules are set out in full in @sec-blp-vehicles. The comparison worth holding in your head:

| | Partnership (PA 1890 defaults) | Private company (Model Articles) |
|---|---|---|
| Who manages | **Every partner** (s.24(5)) | The **board** (MA 3) |
| Ordinary decisions | Majority of partners (s.24(8)) — **one partner, one vote** | Simple majority of directors at a quorate board meeting |
| Change in the nature of the business | **Unanimity** (s.24(8)) | Board decision; objects are unrestricted unless the articles restrict them |
| Admitting a new owner | **Unanimity** (s.24(7)) | Board allotment or transfer, subject to the articles and pre-emption rights |
| Expelling an owner | **Not possible** without express agreement (s.25) | Directors removable by ordinary resolution (s.168); **shareholders cannot be expelled** |
| Binding the business to outsiders | Every partner is an agent (s.5) | The board, and those it authorises; s.40 protects third parties |
| Ending it | Any partner may dissolve a partnership at will by notice (s.26) | Special resolution to wind up voluntarily |

::: {.callout-important title="Exam trap"}
Partnership voting is **per capita**, not by capital or profit share, unless the agreement says
otherwise. A partner with 60% of the capital has **one vote** under s.24(8), the same as a partner with
5%. Company voting is by shares. Mixing the two is a reliable way to lose a mark.
:::

For an LLP, the default regulations reproduce the partnership position — every member may take part in
management, ordinary matters by majority, change in the nature of the business by unanimity, no new
member without unanimity, and no power of expulsion — but with the two differences noted in
@sec-blp-vehicles: a member may resign on reasonable notice, and no member can dissolve the LLP.

## The solicitor's position

**Who is the client?** When a solicitor is instructed by a company, the client is the **company**, not
the director giving the instructions. Where the director's personal interests diverge from the
company's — a substantial property transaction with himself, a loan, an ex gratia payment — the
solicitor must be clear that they act for the company, must not advise the director personally on the
same matter without addressing the conflict, and should ensure that the disinterested members of the
board understand the position.

**Taking instructions from one director.** A solicitor may generally act on instructions from a person
with authority to give them, but should be alert to a director purporting to commit the company to a
transaction that requires a board or members' resolution. Where the transaction plainly requires
approval that has not been obtained, proceeding on one director's say-so risks facilitating a breach of
duty.

**Confidentiality and the board.** Information given to the solicitor by the company is the company's,
not any individual director's. A director who resigns cannot demand the company's confidential
material, and a solicitor should not disclose company information to a former director without
authority.

**When directors and shareholders disagree.** A solicitor acting for the company owes duties to the
company as an entity. Advising a majority shareholder on how to remove the directors, while also acting
for the company, is a conflict; the usual answer is that the solicitor must decline to act for one of
them, and may need to cease acting for both.

## Chapter review

**Q1.** A private company has three directors and four shareholders. One shareholder holds 55%, and the
three directors hold 15% each. The 55% shareholder wishes to (i) remove one of the directors and (ii)
change the company's name. The articles are the unamended Model Articles.

Which of the following correctly identifies the procedure for both?

A. An ordinary resolution by written resolution for (i), and a special resolution by written
resolution for (ii).

B. An ordinary resolution at a general meeting on special notice for (i), and a special resolution
(which may be a written resolution) for (ii) — although with only 55% of the votes she cannot pass the
special resolution.

C. A special resolution for both, at a general meeting.

D. A board resolution for (i) and a special resolution for (ii).

E. An ordinary resolution at a general meeting for both.

**Q2.** A director of a private company arranges for the company to lend him £30,000, repayable in
twelve months, to fund the purchase of a holiday home. The company is not associated with any public
company and is not a money-lending company. The director has no other outstanding transaction with the
company. No members' resolution is passed.

Which of the following is correct?

A. No approval is required, because the loan provisions apply only to public companies and companies
associated with a public company.

B. No approval is required, because the loan falls within the exception in s.207(1) for minor
transactions.

C. Approval by ordinary resolution, supported by a memorandum made available to the members, was
required; the loan is voidable at the company's instance and the director must account for any gain
and indemnify the company for any loss.

D. Approval by special resolution was required, because the loan exceeds £15,000.

E. The loan is prohibited outright and cannot be authorised by any resolution.

**Q3.** The sole director and 100% shareholder of a company, having taken no advice, causes the company
to make a payment that turns out to be a breach of the duty of care in s.174. The company later enters
insolvent liquidation and the liquidator brings a claim.

Which of the following is correct?

A. The director may rely on his own approval as sole shareholder to ratify the breach under s.239.

B. The director may not rely on ratification, because on a resolution under s.239 his own votes as the
director in question are disregarded, and in any event the *Duomatic* principle does not validate acts
that prejudice creditors of an insolvent company.

C. The claim must fail, because a sole director cannot be in breach of duty to a company he wholly
owns.

D. The claim must fail, because the company may indemnify the director under s.234.

E. The claim must succeed in full, because s.1157 relief is available only to non-executive directors.

**Q4.** Which of the following requires filing at Companies House within **21 days**?

A. A special resolution amending the articles.

B. The appointment of a new director.

C. The creation of a charge over the company's property.

D. A return of allotment of shares.

E. The annual accounts of a private company.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answers and explanations"}

**Q1 — B.** Removal of a director requires an ordinary resolution under s.168, which **cannot** be
passed as a written resolution (s.288(2)) and requires special notice (s.312). The 55% holder has
enough votes for an ordinary resolution at a general meeting. Changing the name requires a **special
resolution** (s.77), for which 75% is needed — and 55% is not enough, whether at a meeting or by
written resolution.

- **A** overlooks the s.288(2) exclusion and the 75% threshold.
- **C** applies a special resolution to the removal.
- **D** gives the board a removal power it does not have.
- **E** applies an ordinary resolution to the change of name.

**Q2 — C.** Section 197 applies to **all** companies, private and public alike: a loan to a director
requires approval by ordinary resolution, with a memorandum of the transaction made available to
members for at least 15 days before the meeting and at the meeting. The exception in s.207(1) covers
loans and quasi-loans whose aggregate value does not exceed **£10,000**, and £30,000 exceeds it.
Section 213 makes the unapproved transaction voidable at the company's instance and requires the
director to account for any gain and indemnify the company for any loss.

- **A** confuses s.197 with **ss.198 and 201**. It is **quasi-loans** and **credit transactions** that
  are confined to public companies and their associates. Ordinary loans are caught whatever the company.
- **B** applies the £10,000 exception to a £30,000 loan.
- **D** applies the wrong resolution and the wrong threshold — £15,000 is the s.207(2) limit for
  **credit transactions**, not loans, and the resolution required is an ordinary one.
- **E** invents an absolute prohibition; the point of s.197 is that members may approve.

**Q3 — B.** Two independent obstacles. On a s.239 resolution the votes of the **director in question**
are disregarded, so a sole director-shareholder cannot ratify his own breach by voting his own shares.
And the *Duomatic* principle does not extend to validating acts that prejudice creditors where the
company is insolvent or approaching insolvency.

- **A** ignores s.239(4).
- **C** contradicts *Salomon*: the duty is owed to the company, which is a separate person from its sole
  member.
- **D** misapplies s.234, which permits an indemnity against liability to **third parties**, not to the
  company; s.232 makes an indemnity against liability to the company void.
- **E** invents a restriction on s.1157, which is available to any officer who acted honestly and
  reasonably.

**Q4 — C.** Section 859A: particulars of a charge, with the instrument, must be delivered within **21
days** beginning with the day after the date of creation. This is also the one filing whose omission
has a substantive consequence — the charge becomes void against a liquidator, administrator or creditor
(s.859H).

- **A** — 15 days (s.30).
- **B** — 14 days (s.167).
- **D** — one month (s.555).
- **E** — 9 months after the accounting reference date (s.442).

:::
